newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysians reject Singaporean apology as inadequate.
newsitem.headline: Malaysians reject Singaporean apology as inadequate.

text.p: A growing chorus of opinion in Malaysia at the weekend said Singaporean leader Lee Kuan's Yew's extraordinary apology to the country was inadequate and one official urged the government to review ties.
Lee outraged Malaysians by describing Johor state, just across the Johor Strait from Singapore, as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".

After a day of protests in which Malaysian youths hurled insults at the former Singapore prime minister and Malaysia demanded a retraction, Lee's office said late on Thursday he apologised "unreservedly" for the offence he had caused to the government and people of Malaysia.
But many in Malaysia, noting Lee had not exactly retracted the statement, said the apology alone was not enough.

The chairman of the youth wing of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) on Saturday urged the government to "review the basis of agreement and diplomatic ties" with Singapore.
The government must make a decision on the matter at the next cabinet meeting as "Lee was being too much", the national news agency Bernama quoted Ahmad Zahid Hamidi as saying.
On Friday, an UMNO youth spokesman said the group may sue Singapore's independence leader for libel. Lee is now Senior Minister in the Singaporean government.

Mahathir, who crossed swords with Lee in the historic parliamentary debates that led to Singapore being expelled from the Malaysian Federation in 1965, told reporters on Saturday in the northern state of Perlis he would reserve comment until after Wednesday's cabinet meeting.

"I don't want to talk on it anymore...I want to meet my ministers first," Bernama quoted him as saying. "We have read and heard about (the people's) feelings in the mass media. There is no need for a referendum on it," he added.
Born from the same British imperial legacy and united briefly from 1963 to 1965, the two nations have close-knit economic, political and cultural ties -- and a history of spats.

Singapore imports much of its food, water and raw materials from across the Johor Strait and is among the biggest investors in Malaysia. Tens of thousands of Malaysians fill jobs in the island-state's labour-short economy.
Mahathir said after Lee's apology statement that it was a small step in improving ties, but added: "We in the government have always had problems with Singapore."

UMNO's Ahmad Zahid said Malaysia should review the water agreement and Singapore's use of Malaysian air space. He also urged the government to stop sending Malaysian goods to Singapore for re-export to third countries.

Lee's remarks about Johor were made in a January 27 affidavit in one of 13 libel lawsuits brought against Singapore opposition politician Tang Liang Hong after elections. Tang fled to Johor, saying he had received death threats in Singapore. Lee questioned whether Tang would really be safer in Johor.
A senior official of the Malaysian Chinese Association (MCA), a key partner in Mahathir's National Front coalition government, urged Lee on Saturday to withdraw the affidavit.
Chor Chee Heung, MCA's international bureau chief, also said Lee should have personally apologised instead of issuing a statement through his office.

A. Kadir Jasin, the influential group editor of the New Straits Times publishing house, said in a widely-read Sunday column: "Now that the offensive statement has been pointed out to him in no uncertain terms, and an apology alone is not sufficient, one wonders when Lee will instruct his counsel to remove it from the affidavit."
